questions.question: What are the different fetch strategies for `@OneToMany` in Hibernate — JOIN, SUBSELECT, and SELECT — and how do you choose between them?
questions.title: @OneToMany Fetch Strategies — JOIN, SUBSELECT, SELECT, BatchSize
questions.direct_answer: Hibernate supports four practical fetch strategies for `@OneToMany`. **SELECT (default LAZY)** — 1 query for parents + 1 per parent's collection on access (the classic **N+1**). **JOIN (`@Fetch(JOIN)` / `JOIN FETCH`)** — one query with LEFT JOIN; rows multiply (Cartesian) and **pagination breaks** (`HHH90003004` — Hibernate paginates in memory). **SUBSELECT (`@Fetch(SUBSELECT)`)** — parent query + one follow-up `WHERE parent_id IN (SELECT ... FROM original_query)`; works with pagination. **`@BatchSize(50)`** — reduces N+1 to `ceil(N/50) + 1` via `WHERE parent_id IN (?, ?, ?)` batches; works with pagination. **`FetchType.EAGER` on `@OneToMany` is always wrong** — it forces JOIN on every parent load and silently produces Cartesian products.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of N+1 and the trade-offs between fetch strategies, including pagination compatibility
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using `FetchType.EAGER` on `@OneToMany` thinking it avoids N+1 — instead it causes a JOIN that multiplies rows (Cartesian product)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why JOIN fetch breaks pagination, when SUBSELECT or BatchSize is preferable, and the global `default_batch_fetch_size` setting

sections.title: EAGER `@OneToMany` Doesn't Fix N+1 — It Creates a Cartesian Product
sections.content:
Developers see N+1 on a `@OneToMany` collection and reach for `FetchType.EAGER`, expecting Hibernate to load everything in one query. It does — with a JOIN that **multiplies result rows**. An order with 10 items + 5 payments via two EAGER collections returns 50 rows per order — the Cartesian product explodes silently.

Hibernate offers three fetch strategies for collections: **SELECT** (default lazy — N+1), **JOIN** (one query with a JOIN — Cartesian risk, breaks pagination), and **SUBSELECT** (one extra query with a subselect — no Cartesian, no N+1, but loads all matching collections). A fourth practical strategy is **`@BatchSize`** — batched IN-clause loading that works with pagination.

The right choice depends on whether you need pagination, how many collections you load, and whether you want eager-equivalent behavior. There is **no universally correct strategy**.

sections.title: ER Cardinality of `@OneToMany`/`@ManyToOne`/`@ManyToMany`
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    customer["Customer"] -- "1" --- one1["OneToMany"]
    one1 -- "N" --- order["Order"]
    order -- "N" --- many1["ManyToOne"]
    many1 -- "1" --- customer

    order -- "1" --- one2["OneToMany items"]
    one2 -- "N" --- item["OrderItem"]
    item -- "N" --- many2["ManyToOne product"]
    many2 -- "1" --- product["Product"]

    student["Student"] -- "N" --- mm["ManyToMany via Enrollment"]
    mm -- "N" --- course["Course"]
```

sections.title: SELECT vs JOIN vs SUBSELECT vs BatchSize
sections.content:
Each strategy trades query count, result size, and pagination compatibility.

| Strategy | Queries | Pagination | Cartesian risk | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SELECT (default lazy) | 1 + N | Works | None | Small N, infrequent access |
| JOIN (`@Fetch(JOIN)` / `JOIN FETCH`) | 1 | Breaks (in-memory) | Yes — rows multiply | Single collection, no pagination |
| SUBSELECT (`@Fetch(SUBSELECT)`) | 2 | Works | None | Always need collection across page |
| `@BatchSize(size=50)` | 1 + ceil(N/50) | Works | None | Pagination + general default |

sections.title: Four Strategies, Four SQL Patterns
Why EAGER Is Forbidden and When Each Strategy Wins
sections.content:
**`FetchType.EAGER` on `@OneToMany` is always wrong:**
- Loads the full collection on **every** query that touches the parent.
- Cartesian product when combined with another EAGER collection.
- `findById` loads the entire items table for that order.
- Cannot be overridden per query reliably.
- Pagination silently breaks with `HHH90003004`.

**`DISTINCT` with JOIN FETCH:**
- `select distinct o from Order o join fetch o.items` deduplicates **in Java**, not SQL.
- Add hint `hibernate.query.passDistinctThrough = false` to skip the redundant SQL DISTINCT.

**SUBSELECT vs BatchSize:**
- **SUBSELECT wins** when you consistently need the collection for every parent in the result.
- **BatchSize wins** when collections are sometimes unneeded and when multiple queries hit the same entities.

**`Set` vs `List`:**
- `Set` deduplicates automatically but needs business-key `equals/hashCode`.
- `List` allows duplicates and preserves order; needs DISTINCT on JOIN FETCH.
- `MultipleBagFetchException` fires when fetching two `List` collections — solutions: split queries, use `Set`, or `@BatchSize` on both.

**Watch for:**
- **Cartesian explosions** with two `@OneToMany` JOIN FETCH.
- **`FetchType.EAGER` on `@OneToOne` inverse side** — needs bytecode enhancement to be truly lazy.
- **No SQL count tests** — every critical endpoint should assert query count via `Statistics.getPrepareStatementCount()`.

sections.title: Decision Tree for Fetch Strategy
sections.content:
**Start with the global default:**
- `hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size: 50` in application.yml.

**Per query:**
- **Single-entity detail view (`GET /orders/{id}`)** -> `@EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"customer", "items"})`.
- **Non-paginated list with single association** -> `JOIN FETCH` in JPQL.
- **Paginated list with any collection** -> `@BatchSize` + `Pageable`. **Never `JOIN FETCH` + `Pageable` on a collection.**
- **Always-load-everything for parents+children** -> `@Fetch(SUBSELECT)`.
- **Read-heavy summary endpoint** -> DTO projection; skip entity loading entirely.

**Avoid:**
- `FetchType.EAGER` on `@OneToMany`.
- `JOIN FETCH` of two `@OneToMany` (Cartesian or `MultipleBagFetchException`).
- `findAll()` without `Pageable` on a production table.
- Cascading JOIN FETCHes without explicit `DISTINCT`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`FetchType.EAGER` on `@OneToMany`** is always an anti-pattern.
- **`@BatchSize(50)`** is the pragmatic default — pagination-safe, fixes N+1.
- **JOIN FETCH + Pageable** triggers `HHH90003004` and paginates in memory.
- **SUBSELECT** issues one follow-up with the parent IDs — works with pagination.
- **`@EntityGraph`** is the modern, declarative way to fetch associations per query.
- **Global `default_batch_fetch_size: 50`** in application.yml fixes most N+1 bugs.
- **DTO projections** beat entity loading for read-heavy summaries.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Hibernate has four practical fetch strategies for `@OneToMany` collections.

**SELECT — the default LAZY:**
- One query for parents, one extra per parent's collection on access — N+1
- Acceptable only when N is small or access is rare

**JOIN FETCH:**
- One query with LEFT JOIN — zero N+1
- Rows multiply — Cartesian product with multiple collections
- Pagination breaks — `HHH90003004`, Hibernate paginates in memory

**SUBSELECT (`@Fetch(SUBSELECT)`):**
- One query for parents + one follow-up `WHERE parent_id IN (SELECT...)`
- Works with pagination, no Cartesian risk
- Best when you always need the collection across the entire page

**`@BatchSize(50)`:**
- Reduces N+1 to `ceil(N/50)+1` via batched IN-clause queries
- Pagination-safe, the pragmatic default
- Set globally with `hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size: 50`

**Avoid:**
- `FetchType.EAGER` on `@OneToMany` — silently produces Cartesian products
- JOIN FETCH of two `@OneToMany` — `MultipleBagFetchException` or row explosion
- JOIN FETCH + Pageable on a collection — Hibernate paginates in memory

questions.question: How do you map JPA entity relationships — `@OneToMany`, `@ManyToOne`, `@ManyToMany`?
questions.title: JPA Entity Relationships — Owning Side, Inverse Side, Mapping
questions.direct_answer: JPA relationships have two concepts that explain every mapping bug: the **owning side** (holds the foreign key column) and the **inverse side** (declared with `mappedBy`). For `@ManyToOne`/`@OneToMany`: **`@ManyToOne` is always the owning side** — the FK lives on its table. **`@OneToMany(mappedBy=...)`** is the inverse — it reads but doesn't write. **Missing `mappedBy` is the classic bug** — Hibernate creates an extra join table instead of using the FK. For `@ManyToMany`: one side owns the join table; **changes to the inverse side are silently ignored**. Bidirectional relationships need helper methods that update both sides. Collection choice: **`Set` for `@ManyToMany`** (List causes delete-all-and-reinsert), **`List` with `@OrderColumn`** when order matters, **business-key `equals/hashCode`** (never ID-based) to survive the unsaved-then-saved transition.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands owning vs inverse side and can map relationships correctly
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not setting `mappedBy` on `@OneToMany` — Hibernate creates an extra join table instead of using the FK on the `@ManyToOne` side
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why bidirectional `@ManyToMany` should use `Set`, the junction-entity pattern, and the business-key `equals/hashCode` rule

sections.title: Missing `mappedBy` Creates an Extra Join Table — The Most Common Mapping Mistake
sections.content:
The most common JPA relationship bug is `@OneToMany` without `mappedBy`. Hibernate interprets this as a **unidirectional** one-to-many backed by a join table — an extra `order_items` table with `order_id` and `item_id`. Adding `mappedBy = "order"` tells Hibernate the `@ManyToOne` on `Item` is the owning side and the FK lives directly on `items`.

The **owning side** controls the foreign key column in the database. For `@ManyToOne`/`@OneToMany`, the owning side is always `@ManyToOne` — it maps to the actual FK. The `@OneToMany(mappedBy=...)` is the **inverse side** — reads the relationship but doesn't write it.

This distinction means **adding to `order.getItems()` without setting `item.setOrder(order)` doesn't persist the relationship.** Only changes on the owning side reach the database. Bidirectional relationships require helper methods that synchronize both sides in Java code.

sections.title: `@ManyToMany` with `Set` — and Why `List` Causes Duplicate Rows
sections.content:
**Default behavior:**
- `@ManyToMany` creates a join table automatically.
- `Student` and `Course` produce a `student_courses(student_id, course_id)` table.
- The owning side (whichever lacks `mappedBy`) controls the join table.

**Why `Set<Course>` not `List<Course>`:**
- With **`List`**, removing one course triggers `DELETE FROM student_courses WHERE student_id=?` then re-INSERT of the survivors — O(n) writes.
- With **`Set`**, only the affected row is inserted or deleted.
- On a student with 50 courses, removing one course = **50 DELETEs + 49 INSERTs vs 1 DELETE**.

**Bidirectional sync helper:**
- Always provide `addCourse(course)` and `removeCourse(course)` that update both sides.
- Without sync, the in-memory state diverges from database state inside the same transaction.
- Hibernate persists what the **owning side** says — the inverse-side change is silently lost.

sections.title: Relationship Types — Owning Side, SQL Generated, Pitfalls
sections.content:
Five JPA relationship annotations and what they generate at the SQL level.

| Annotation | Owning side | SQL generated | Pitfall | Idiomatic usage |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `@ManyToOne` | Always owner | FK column on child table | Default EAGER — override to LAZY | `@ManyToOne(fetch=LAZY) @JoinColumn(name="order_id") Order order;` |
| `@OneToMany(mappedBy=...)` | Never owner (inverse) | No FK; reads child's FK | Missing `mappedBy` creates join table | `@OneToMany(mappedBy="order", cascade={PERSIST,MERGE}, orphanRemoval=true) Set<Item> items;` |
| `@OneToOne` | Either | FK on owner's table | Default EAGER, hard to LAZY on inverse | `@OneToOne(fetch=LAZY, mappedBy="user") UserProfile profile;` |
| `@ManyToMany` | Side without `mappedBy` | `@JoinTable` with two FKs | `List` causes delete-all+reinsert | `Set<Tag> tags;` — never `List<Tag>` |
| Junction entity | Composed `@ManyToOne` x 2 | Real entity with attrs | Forgotten when relation needs metadata | `@Entity Enrollment { @ManyToOne Student s; @ManyToOne Course c; Instant enrolledAt; }` |

sections.title: Bidirectional Sync Helper + Junction Entity Pattern
`equals`/`hashCode`, `Set` vs `List`, and the Cascade.REMOVE Trap
sections.content:
**When mapping helps:**
- Correct `mappedBy` and FK placement gives clean SQL with no extra tables.
- Bidirectional sync helpers keep object graphs consistent.
- `Set` for `@ManyToMany` produces minimal DELETE/INSERT footprint.

**When mapping hurts:**
- **ID-based `equals/hashCode`** breaks when entities are added to a `Set` before save — unsaved id is null, after save id changes, `set.contains(entity)` returns false.
- **`@ManyToMany` with `List`** = delete-all-and-reinsert on any change.
- **`CascadeType.REMOVE` on `@ManyToMany`** = catastrophic — deleting a student deletes shared courses.

**Watch for:**
- **Always use a business key or UUID** for `equals/hashCode`, never the ID.
- **`FetchType.EAGER` defaults** on `@ManyToOne` and `@OneToOne` — override to LAZY explicitly.
- **`@OneToOne` inverse LAZY** doesn't actually lazy without bytecode enhancement.
- **Cascade flows parent-to-child** — never cascade from `@ManyToOne` to its parent.
- **Modeling the junction as an entity** the moment any metadata is needed.
- **Never `cascade = ALL` across `@ManyToMany`** — REMOVE inside ALL deletes shared rows.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@OneToMany` without `mappedBy`** creates a join table — always add it.
- **`@ManyToMany` should use `Set`** — `List` causes delete-all-and-reinsert.
- **Bidirectional relationships need sync helpers** — Hibernate persists only the owning side.
- **`@JoinTable` controls junction table naming** — customize to avoid schema conflicts.
- **Model `@ManyToMany` as a junction entity** when the relationship has attributes.
- **`@ManyToOne` and `@OneToOne` default EAGER** — override to LAZY.
- **Business-key `equals/hashCode`** — never ID-based; survives the unsaved->saved transition.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
JPA relationships hinge on understanding owning side vs inverse side.

**Owning vs inverse:**
- The owning side holds the FK column — for `@OneToMany`/`@ManyToOne`, that's `@ManyToOne`
- The inverse side declares `mappedBy` — reads the relationship, never writes it
- Hibernate persists only changes made to the owning side

**The `mappedBy` bug:**
- `@OneToMany` without `mappedBy` creates a third join table — usually wrong
- Add `mappedBy = "order"` to use the FK already on the child table

**`@ManyToMany` with `Set`:**
- `List` triggers DELETE-all + INSERT-survivors on any change
- `Set` only inserts/deletes the affected row
- Use `Set<Course>` always; use a junction entity when the relationship has metadata

**Bidirectional sync helpers:**
- `addItem` and `removeItem` methods that set both sides
- Without them, in-memory state diverges from database state in the same transaction

**`equals`/`hashCode`:**
- Never base on the ID — ID is null before save, set after
- Use a business key or a UUID generated in the constructor

**Defaults to override:**
- `@ManyToOne` and `@OneToOne` default EAGER — make them LAZY
- `@OneToMany` defaults LAZY — keep it that way

questions.question: What are JPA cascade types and `orphanRemoval`, and when should you use each?
questions.title: JPA Cascade Types and `orphanRemoval` — When to Use Each
questions.direct_answer: JPA cascade types propagate entity lifecycle operations (`persist`, `merge`, `remove`, `refresh`, `detach`) from a parent to its children. **`PERSIST`** — saving the parent saves new children. **`MERGE`** — merging the parent merges children. **`REMOVE`** — deleting the parent deletes all children (**catastrophic on `@ManyToMany`** because it deletes shared entities). **`ALL`** combines all five. **`orphanRemoval = true`** is a stricter, collection-level trigger — it fires whenever a child is removed from the collection, even if the parent still exists. Distinction: **cascade REMOVE deletes children when the parent is deleted; orphanRemoval deletes children when removed from the collection OR when parent is deleted**. Safe default for owned `@OneToMany`: `cascade = {PERSIST, MERGE}, orphanRemoval = true`. **Never cascade REMOVE across `@ManyToMany`**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the difference between cascade REMOVE and orphanRemoval, and when each is appropriate
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using `CascadeType.ALL` on `@ManyToMany` — deleting one student cascades to delete courses, which cascades to delete other students enrolled
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain orphanRemoval as collection-level ON DELETE CASCADE, the ghost-entity bug from MERGE, and the cascade decision tree by relationship type

sections.title: `CascadeType.ALL` on `@ManyToMany` Deletes Shared Entities
sections.content:
Cascade types propagate lifecycle operations from a parent to its children. `PERSIST` and `MERGE` are convenient and safe. **`REMOVE` and `ALL` are where the danger lives.**

On a `@OneToMany` (parent owns children), `CascadeType.REMOVE` is fine — deleting an order deletes its line items. On a `@ManyToMany`, it's catastrophic. Deleting a student with `cascade = ALL` on `courses` deletes the courses themselves, and other students enrolled in those courses lose them. **One delete can empty the database.**

**`orphanRemoval = true`** is the collection-level delete trigger.
- It deletes children when they're removed from the parent's collection — `order.getItems().remove(item)` deletes the item from the database.
- Without it, removing from the collection only nullifies the FK; the orphan stays as a ghost row.

sections.title: cascade REMOVE vs `orphanRemoval` — The Critical Distinction
sections.content:
Both delete children, but at different trigger points.

**`cascade = REMOVE`** fires when:
- `em.remove(parent)` is called.
- Parent deletion cascades to all children.
- Removing an item from the collection without deleting the parent **does not** delete the item — it leaves an orphan with a null FK.

**`orphanRemoval = true`** fires when:
- A child is removed from the parent's collection (`order.getItems().remove(item)`).
- The parent is deleted (implicit cascade REMOVE).
- Both triggers in one annotation.

**Use `orphanRemoval = true` when** children have no meaning without the parent — line items, phone numbers, addresses on a user.

**Don't use `orphanRemoval` when** children can exist independently — tags on an article, categories on a product — because removing from the collection would delete the shared entity.

**Safe default for owned `@OneToMany`:**
```java
@OneToMany(mappedBy = "order",
           cascade = {CascadeType.PERSIST, CascadeType.MERGE},
           orphanRemoval = true)
Set<OrderItem> items;
```

sections.title: All Cascade Types + `orphanRemoval`
sections.content:
Six cascade options plus `orphanRemoval`, mapped to the EntityManager operation that triggers them.

| Cascade | Triggering op | Effect | Safe on `@OneToMany`? | Safe on `@ManyToMany`? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PERSIST | `em.persist(parent)` | INSERT new children | Yes | Only when children are new |
| MERGE | `em.merge(parent)` | Re-attach / sync children | Yes | Can resurrect deleted children |
| REMOVE | `em.remove(parent)` | DELETE children | Yes (owned) | DELETES SHARED ENTITIES |
| REFRESH | `em.refresh(parent)` | SELECT child state | Yes | Yes |
| DETACH | `em.detach(parent)` | Remove from context | Yes | Yes |
| ALL | Any of the above | All effects | Owned only | Never |
| `orphanRemoval=true` | Removed from collection | DELETE child on flush | Yes | Not applicable |

sections.title: Cascade Patterns in Practice
Detached Entities, Merge Pitfalls, and the Cascade Decision Tree
sections.content:
**When cascade helps:**
- **Owned children lifecycle** — saving/deleting a parent should propagate to its children.
- **Junction entities** — `cascade = ALL` is safe because the junction is owned.
- **`orphanRemoval`** acts like collection-level ON DELETE CASCADE.

**When cascade hurts:**
- **`@ManyToMany cascade = REMOVE`** deletes shared entities.
- **`MERGE` resurrects deleted children** — the 'ghost entity' bug when REST clients send full payloads with previously-removed children still present.
- **`PERSIST` with already-persisted children** throws `TransientPropertyValueException`.

**Watch for:**
- **Cascade from `@ManyToOne` to its parent** — almost always wrong; cascade flows parent-to-child.
- **`orphanRemoval` on a unidirectional `@OneToMany`** with a join table doesn't work — needs a single owner.
- **REST update endpoints sending full payloads** — load fresh and apply specific changes; don't blindly merge a DTO-derived detached entity.

**Decision tree by relationship:**
- **`@ManyToMany`** -> no cascade on REMOVE/ALL; use `PERSIST, MERGE` only if children always new.
- **Owned `@OneToMany`** -> `cascade = {PERSIST, MERGE}, orphanRemoval = true`.
- **Shared children** -> no cascade or `PERSIST, MERGE` only.
- **Junction entity** -> `cascade = ALL, orphanRemoval = true` on parent->junction; no cascade on junction->other side.
- **`@ManyToOne`** -> almost never cascade; LAZY fetch and save the parent independently.

sections.title: Choosing the Cascade Set
sections.content:
**Use `cascade = {PERSIST, MERGE}, orphanRemoval = true` when:**
- Children have no meaning without the parent.
- Lifecycle is fully owned by the parent.
- Examples: line items, phone numbers, addresses, user settings.

**Use no cascade (or `PERSIST, MERGE` only) when:**
- Children are shared across multiple parents.
- Examples: tags on articles, categories on products, courses on students.

**Use `cascade = ALL, orphanRemoval = true` only when:**
- The associated entity is a true junction owned by the parent.
- Example: `Student -> Enrollment` where `Enrollment` belongs to one student.

**Never:**
- `cascade = REMOVE` or `ALL` across `@ManyToMany`.
- Cascade from `@ManyToOne` toward the parent.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`CascadeType.ALL` on `@ManyToMany`** can delete shared entities — never use it.
- **Safe default for owned `@OneToMany`** is `{PERSIST, MERGE} + orphanRemoval = true`.
- **`orphanRemoval`** deletes children removed from the collection or when parent is deleted.
- **`orphanRemoval` only works on the owning side** with `mappedBy` or `@JoinColumn`.
- **`MERGE` can resurrect children** removed in the database but still in the detached entity.
- **Cascade flows parent-to-child** — never cascade from `@ManyToOne`.
- **Junction entities** can safely use `cascade = ALL` — they're owned by one parent.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Cascade types propagate JPA operations from a parent to its associated children. Choosing the wrong one is one of the easiest ways to delete data unintentionally.

**What each cascade does:**
- PERSIST — saving the parent saves new children
- MERGE — merging the parent merges children
- REMOVE — deleting the parent deletes children
- REFRESH — refreshing the parent re-loads children
- ALL — all of the above

**The `@ManyToMany` REMOVE trap:**
- `@ManyToMany(cascade = REMOVE)` on `Student.courses` deletes the courses themselves
- Other students lose those courses too — catastrophic
- Never cascade REMOVE or ALL across `@ManyToMany`

**`orphanRemoval = true`:**
- Collection-level ON DELETE CASCADE
- `order.getItems().remove(item)` triggers DELETE on the item
- Also fires when parent is deleted
- Only works on the owning side with `mappedBy` or `@JoinColumn`

**Safe defaults:**
- Owned children -> `cascade = {PERSIST, MERGE}, orphanRemoval = true`
- Shared children -> no cascade or `PERSIST, MERGE` only
- Junction entities -> `cascade = ALL, orphanRemoval = true`
- `@ManyToOne` -> almost never cascade

beats.text: Cascade types propagate lifecycle operations from a parent to its children. PERSIST and MERGE are convenient and safe. REMOVE and ALL are where the danger lives. On a @OneToMany (parent owns children), CascadeType.REMOVE is fine — deleting an order deletes its line items. On a @ManyToMany, it's catastrophic. Deleting a student with cascade = ALL on courses deletes the courses themselves, and other students enrolled in those courses lose them. One delete can empty the database. orphanRemoval = true is.

beats.text: Cascade types propagate lifecycle operations from a parent to its children. PERSIST and MERGE are convenient and safe. REMOVE and ALL are where the danger lives. On a @OneToMany (parent owns children), CascadeType.REMOVE is fine — deleting an order deletes its line items. On a @ManyToMany, it's catastrophic. Deleting a student with cascade = ALL on courses deletes the courses themselves, and other students enrolled in those courses lose them. One delete can empty the database. orphanRemoval = true is the collection-level delete trigger. It deletes children when they're removed from the parent's collection — order.getItems().remove(item) deletes the item from the database. Without it, removing from the collection only nullifies the FK; the orphan stays as a ghost row.
